question: A loop over `float *out, const float *in` with a runtime length n is not vectorized at `gcc -O2` but is at -O3. What is the most likely reason?
options: -O2 does not support SIMD instructions
-O2's very-cheap cost model rejects loops that need a runtime alias check
Floats can never be vectorized at -O2
The loop needs -march=native first
explain: With runtime n and two pointers that may overlap, vectorizing needs a runtime overlap check. The very-cheap model used at -O2 refuses any runtime alias check (and, before GCC 15, any loop needing a scalar epilogue); -O3's dynamic model accepts them. restrict (plus a known trip count on GCC 14 and older) can make -O2 vectorize it.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
question: You build a CLI tool on a new workstation with `-O2 -march=native` and publish the binary for all Linux x86-64 users. What is the main risk?
options: It runs slower on older CPUs
It produces different numeric results on AMD
It may use instructions older CPUs lack, so it fails to run there
Nothing, -march only affects scheduling
explain: -march=native enables every extension of the build machine, and GCC's manual warns the result might not run elsewhere. For a distributed binary use the default target, a psABI level like x86-64-v2 or v3 that you document, or runtime dispatch (ship several versions of the hot code and pick one at startup from the CPU's features). -mtune changes scheduling only.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Coordinates: grounding a click and scaling it to the real display
question: Clicks land in the right area but often miss very small targets. Scaling is verified correct. Which fix matches the docs' guidance?
options: Send the screenshot at a higher resolution than the image limit so the API keeps detail
Switch the aspect ratio of the screenshot to 1:1 so the model counts pixels more easily
Keep zoom enabled so the model can inspect the region at full resolution, and keep the aspect ratio when resizing
Retry each click three times at random offsets of a few pixels
explain: The docs attribute right-area misses to tiny targets, detail lost when downscaling a large source, or distorted aspect ratio, and suggest zoom, cropping or capturing at lower DPI (dots per inch), and preserving aspect ratio. Oversized images are rejected, not kept. Random retries can click the wrong thing.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
question: Your lock-free queue test passed 50,000 times on an x86 laptop. A teammate says it is now safe to ship to Arm servers. What is the strongest objection?
options: 50,000 runs is too few; 5 million runs would be enough
x86 hardware keeps more orderings than Arm, so a missing Release or Acquire may simply be invisible there and still break on Arm
The test should have been run in debug mode instead of release mode
Lock-free code cannot be tested at all, only proven
explain: Running more often only samples more schedules of the same hardware memory model. Weak-ordering bugs that x86's stronger hardware ordering hides have probability zero there, so no count of x86 runs covers them. A tool that models the language memory model, like loom, can explore those executions.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
question: A CI job runs your C++ service's integration tests under `-fsanitize=thread` and reports nothing for months. Which statement is justified?
options: The service is free of data races
TSan is misconfigured, since every large program has races
The service cannot deadlock
No data race occurred, unordered by happens-before, on the code paths and synchronization these tests exercised
explain: TSan is a dynamic detector: it is precise about what it saw but blind to paths that never ran and to races hidden by incidental synchronization in this run. Clean reports are evidence about the executed paths only.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
question: You need a one-step text-to-image model and have no budget for training a new diffusion model, but you do have a strong pretrained latent diffusion model with classifier-free guidance. Which approach fits best?
options: Latent consistency distillation (LCM) or adversarial diffusion distillation from that model
Consistency training from scratch on pixels
Progressive distillation from 8192 steps in pixel space
Plain L2 regression from noise to random images
explain: LCM and ADD both start from an existing latent diffusion teacher and target 1 to 4 steps; LCM distills the guided ODE directly (about 32 A100 hours for its 768x768 model). CT from scratch means training a new model; PD takes many halving stages; noise-to-random-image regression learns the mean.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Why quorum overlap alone is not linearizable, and the fix
question: A Dynamo-style store uses N=3, W=2, R=2 with last-write-wins timestamps and no read write-back. Which anomaly can still occur?
options: A read missing a write that completed long ago
Two reads in sequence, the second returning an older value than the first while a write is in flight
A read returning a value that was never written
Writes being lost because W is not equal to N
explain: With W + R greater than N, every completed write is seen by later quorum reads. But during a write that has reached only some replicas, one read can see it and a later read can miss it, exactly the R2 then R3 pattern. ABD's write-back closes that gap.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Virtual nodes: many tokens per server smooth out the load
question: You run 20 nodes with 1 token each and see one node at 3x average load. Which change reduces the spread of per-node load most directly?
options: Switch the key hash from MD5 to a faster hash
Give each node about 100 tokens (virtual nodes)
Add 5 more nodes with 1 token each
Replicate every key to 3 nodes
explain: Spread comes from uneven arc sizes. With T tokens per node the relative spread falls roughly like 1/sqrt(T), so 100 tokens cuts it to around 10%. A different hash function does not change the geometry, more single-token nodes stay just as uneven, and replication multiplies storage without evening out arcs.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Decay functions turn distance and recency into smooth scores
question: With gauss on distance, offset 5 km, scale 20 km, decay 0.5: what does a candidate 25 km away score, and what does one 4 km away score?
explain: At 25 km, d = 25 - 5 = 20 = scale, so the score equals decay, 0.5. At 4 km the candidate is inside the offset, d = 0, so the score is 1.0.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Arc consistency: AC-3 prunes domains before guessing
question: X and Y have domain {1,2,3} and the only constraint is X < Y. What does AC-3 leave?
options: X {1,2,3}, Y {1,2,3}, because no value is fixed yet
X {1,2}, Y {1,2,3}, because only the arc (X,Y) is revised
explain: Revising (X,Y) deletes X=3 (no larger Y); revising (Y,X) deletes Y=1 (no smaller X). X=1 is supported by Y=2 or 3, and X=2 by Y=3, so nothing else goes. AC-3 keeps every value that appears in some solution of a single constraint; it does not pick a solution.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
question: Why is a container escape usually considered easier to find than a VM escape?
options: Container images are public
Containers share the host kernel, whose large system call interface is directly reachable, while a VM's guest talks to a much smaller hypervisor interface
Containers are written in Go
VMs encrypt their memory
explain: A container's processes make system calls straight into the host kernel, so any kernel bug reachable through those calls is a candidate. A VM's kernel is separate; escaping needs a bug in the hypervisor's narrower interface.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime settings that switch the fences off
question: A team says their pod needs `privileged: true` only to change one network setting. What is the better request?
options: Disable seccomp but keep capabilities default
Keep privileged; it is the same thing
Use hostPID instead
Add only the specific capability needed (for example NET_ADMIN) and keep seccomp, AppArmor or SELinux on
explain: The Kubernetes docs advise granting specific capabilities rather than privileged mode, because privileged also removes seccomp and LSM confinement and grants every capability.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
question: Five apps in namespace shop all use the default service account. An admin binds a Role allowing `get secrets` to it so one app can read its config. What changed for the other four?
options: All four can now read Secrets in shop, because they run as the same identity
Only if they mount the Secret
Only pods created after the binding are affected
Nothing, roles are per app
explain: RBAC grants rights to the identity, and all five pods share it. Give each app its own service account so a binding affects only the app that needs it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Exposed dashboards, kubelets and Docker APIs
question: A self-built cluster's kubelets run with flags only, no config file, and `--anonymous-auth` and `--authorization-mode` are not set. Port 10250 is reachable from the internet. What can an unauthenticated stranger do?
options: Only list pod names
Run commands in containers through the kubelet API, since anonymous requests are allowed and authorization defaults to AlwaysAllow
Nothing, because port 10250 uses TLS
Only read node metrics
explain: The kubelet auth docs give these defaults: anonymous requests accepted, AlwaysAllow authorization. TLS encrypts the connection but does not authenticate the caller. This is the Hildegard entry point.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: A container is a process with a narrowed view
question: A process inside a pid namespace runs the equivalent of kill -TERM 1, aiming at its own init process, which has installed no SIGTERM handler. What happens?
options: The signal is delivered, pid 1 exits, and the kernel SIGKILLs the rest of the namespace
Nothing reaches pid 1: a namespace member may only signal its init process for signals that init handles
The signal is redirected to the host's pid 1
The kernel rejects the call because pid 1 is in another namespace
explain: pid_namespaces(7) says only signals for which the init process has established a handler can be sent to it by other members of the namespace, and that this holds even for privileged processes. It exists to stop a container accidentally killing its own init. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are forced through only when sent from an ancestor namespace.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Probes, Services and DNS: liveness is not readiness
question: An application takes 40 s to warm its caches. Its only probe is a liveness probe with initialDelaySeconds 10, periodSeconds 5 and failureThreshold 3. What do you observe?
options: The pod becomes Ready at 40 s, because liveness failures only affect traffic
The container is restarted at about 20 s and keeps restarting, because the budget is 10 + 3 x 5 = 25 s
The pod stays Pending until the probe succeeds
Nothing: the kubelet waits for a first success before it starts counting failures
explain: Probes at 10, 15 and 20 seconds all fail, which reaches failureThreshold, so the kubelet restarts the container and the clock starts over. The fix is a startup probe on the same endpoint: periodSeconds 10 with failureThreshold 30 allows 300 s, succeeds at 40 s, and only then lets liveness and readiness begin.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries
question: Which turn in the session is a replace rather than an add?
options: T2 now only remote ones
T3 actually make it staff level
T4 drop the salary limit
T1 the first search
explain: Level already held senior and changes to staff, so it is a replace. T2 fills a null slot (add), T4 empties a slot (remove), and T1 is four adds onto an empty state.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Poking the chain: truncate it, break it, reword it
question: You suspect a model hides information in its word choices. Which intervention tests this most directly, and what result would support your suspicion?
options: Filler tokens; accuracy rises with more dots
Early answering; the answer is fixed at step 0
Adding mistakes; answers ignore the mistake
Paraphrasing; accuracy drops when the same content is reworded
explain: Encoded reasoning lives in the exact phrasing, so rewording the content while keeping its meaning should destroy it and cost accuracy. Lanham et al. saw no such drop. Filler tokens test hidden compute, not hidden encoding; the other two test post-hoc reasoning.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Building and scoring a CoT monitor
question: A monitor flags 2% of clean runs and catches 90% of hacks. Hacks occur in 0.5% of runs. About what share of flags are real hacks?
options: About 18%
About 90%
About 2%
About 50%
explain: precision = 0.005 x 0.9 / (0.005 x 0.9 + 0.995 x 0.02) = 0.0045 / (0.0045 + 0.0199) = 0.184. 90% is recall, not precision. At this base rate, false alarms outnumber real hacks more than 4 to 1.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Pinned host memory: the precondition for overlap
question: On which system does switching from pageable to pinned host memory help least, and why?
options: The laptop, because its link is slower so the copy dominates either way
Neither; the ratio is a property of the PCIe generation, not the host
The desktop, because a faster GPU hides the staging copy behind the kernel
The desktop, because its CPU runs the driver's staging memcpy fast enough that staging was not the bottleneck
explain: Pageable transfers were 5.369 GB/s on the desktop against 2.308 GB/s on the laptop, so the desktop's staging memcpy was already near link speed and pinning only added 1.15x there, against 2.50x on the laptop. The bottleneck being removed is host-side, which is why the benefit is a property of the host.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: A worked pipeline: four chunks, and the copy-bound crossover
question: Same pipeline, but you move to a link that is twice as fast, so H2D per chunk drops from 4.00 to 2.00 ms and D2H to 0.125 ms. What is the new 4-chunk time?
options: 14.13 ms, half of before
24.00 ms, the kernel total exactly
26.13 ms, and the speedup over the new serial time drops to 1.24x
28.25 ms, unchanged, because the kernel was already the bottleneck
explain: Makespan is sum + (n-1) x max = (2.00 + 6.00 + 0.125) + 3 x 6.00 = 26.13 ms. New serial time is 4 x 8.125 = 32.50 ms, so the speedup from overlap falls to 1.24x. Faster links make the absolute time better and the overlap win smaller, because there is less copy time left to hide.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Host memory as a tier: unified memory, zero-copy and offloading
question: A kernel reads a 4 KB block of parameters exactly once per launch, with coalesced loads, and the CPU rewrites the block between launches. Which home fits best?
options: Mapped pinned host memory: each byte crosses the link once, inside the kernel, with no separate copy to schedule
Managed memory with no hints, so pages migrate on demand every launch
Pageable malloc memory passed to cudaMemcpyAsync on a side stream
Copy it once at startup and never again
explain: The best practices guide's condition for zero-copy is data read or written only once with coalesced accesses, which this is. Managed memory would fault and migrate pages back and forth every launch. A pageable source makes cudaMemcpyAsync synchronous. Copying once is wrong because the CPU changes the data every launch.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
question: A query is 20 tokens and a passage is 600 tokens. Using a BERT tokenizer with max_length 512 and truncation=True, how many passage tokens remain?
explain: Three special tokens ([CLS] and two [SEP]) plus 20 query tokens use 23 positions, leaving 512 - 23 = 489 for the passage. longest_first trims the longer side, which is the passage.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
question: Why does Margin-MSE train on the score difference instead of asking the student to reproduce the teacher's raw score?
options: Because the teacher's raw scores are not available after training
Because MSE cannot be computed on raw scores
Because the margin is always positive
Because different architectures produce scores on very different ranges, and ranking only depends on order and gaps
explain: The paper observed that cross-encoders, dot-product models and others have distinct score ranges. Matching margins lets the student keep its natural range while learning the teacher's preferences. The margin can even be negative when the teacher disagrees with the label.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key
question: Two ciphertexts were made with the same one-time pad. What can Eve compute without knowing the key?
options: Nothing: each ciphertext is perfectly secret
The key itself, directly
Only the lengths of the messages
The XOR of the two plaintexts
explain: XORing the ciphertexts cancels the key and leaves m1 XOR m2. From there, guessing likely words in one message reveals the other. The key itself only falls out once Eve also knows a plaintext.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Hash functions: fingerprints, avalanche and the birthday bound
question: Which property must a hash have so that nobody can create two different contracts with the same digest, one innocent and one malicious?
options: Preimage resistance
Second-preimage resistance
Avalanche effect
Collision resistance
explain: The attacker controls both documents, so they only need any pair that collides: that is collision resistance, the property MD5 and SHA-1 lost (next lesson).

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
question: Why did Debian's broken generator still produce different keys on different runs, hiding the bug for almost two years?
options: The kernel added entropy later anyway
OpenSSL used the time of day
SSH re-randomised the keys
The process ID was still mixed in, giving about 32,767 variants
explain: Russ Cox notes the PID kept the output from being completely deterministic. If every key had been identical, the bug would likely have been caught quickly.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto
question: In TLS 1.3, which message stops a man in the middle from substituting their own Diffie-Hellman key share?
options: ClientHello
The AEAD tag on application data
The server's random value
CertificateVerify, the server's signature over the handshake
explain: The key shares are just DH values. CertificateVerify signs the transcript, including them, with the key the CA vouched for, so substituted shares fail verification.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Bleichenbacher and ROBOT: retiring RSA key exchange
question: ROBOT's authors could make facebook.com's key sign a message. Why did they say the certificate did not need to be revoked?
options: Because Facebook's certificate had already expired
Because the attack used the server as an oracle to perform operations, without extracting the private key
Because signatures made with a Bleichenbacher oracle are invalid
Because RSA keys cannot be revoked
explain: A Bleichenbacher oracle makes the server's key decrypt or sign attacker-chosen values one step at a time, but the key never leaves the server. Fixing the server (or removing RSA key exchange) closes the oracle; the key stays secret.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Secret-dependent timing: comparisons, Minerva and TPM-Fail
question: A team replaces `==` with this check: `return sum(x != y for x, y in zip(a, b)) == 0`. It visits every byte. Is it a good fix for comparing HMAC tags?
options: Yes, it is exactly as good as hmac.compare_digest
No: summing is slower than ==
No: zip silently stops at the shorter input, and hand-written loops are not guaranteed constant time; use hmac.compare_digest
Yes, as long as tags are hex strings
explain: zip stops at the shorter argument, so a short or empty tag can compare equal to a prefix (an empty tag passes). Interpreter and compiler details can also reintroduce timing differences. The standard library function is designed for this job.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Downgrade and protocol confusion: one key, one purpose
question: A team signs both webhook payloads and password-reset links with one Ed25519 key and no labels. What is the risk?
options: A signature produced for one message type may be accepted where the other is expected, if an attacker can get suitable bytes signed
Ed25519 cannot sign URLs
The key will wear out twice as fast
None, signatures are always bound to their purpose
explain: Signatures bind to bytes, not to meaning. Separate keys, or a purpose label inside the signed data, ensure a webhook signature can never be presented as a reset link signature.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning
question: You compose a data tensor A with B and get R = A o B. Which property does the CuTe documentation guarantee?
options: R has the same shape as A
R is always injective
R(i) = A(B(i)) for all i in B's domain, and R accepts B's coordinates
R has the same strides as B
explain: Composition's post-conditions are compatible(B, R) and R(i) == A(B(i)). B defines the domain, so R takes B's coordinates; A defines where those land.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
question: Why can't a CPU vendor simply add many more DDR5 channels to every socket?
options: DDR5 does not support more than two channels per socket
More channels would make memory non-coherent
Each DDR5 channel is a wide parallel interface that needs many pins (Sun et al. cite 288 per channel), and the package pin budget is fixed
Linux cannot address more than eight memory channels
explain: DDR is a wide parallel interface. Capacity and bandwidth scale with the number of channels, and each channel eats a lot of pins. A serial CXL link delivers more bandwidth per pin, which is why it is attractive for expansion.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
question: TPP does not promote a slow-tier page on its first NUMA hinting fault if the page is on the inactive LRU list. What problem does this avoid?
options: Deadlock between the fault handler and reclaim
Ping-pong: an infrequently used page is promoted, then quickly demoted again, wasting migration bandwidth
Running out of tier-16 memory
Breaking cache coherence on the CXL link
explain: A single touch does not prove a page is hot. Promoting it would push something else out of DRAM, and under pressure the promoted page would soon be demoted again. Requiring the page to be on the active LRU adds hysteresis: a page must show repeated use before it moves, so it stops flipping back and forth.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: View source is not hacking: the Missouri teachers' SSNs (2021)
question: Which statement about Base64 is correct?
options: It is a weak form of encryption that needs a short key
It is an encoding that anyone can reverse without a key, so it protects nothing
It is a hash, so the original cannot be recovered
It is only used for images
explain: Base64 (RFC 4648) maps bytes to 64 printable characters so they survive text channels. Decoding needs no secret. When officials said the reporter had 'unencrypted the source code' or 'decoded the HTML source code', they made an ordinary step sound like an attack.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Copyright and trade secrets: DMCA section 1201 and Megamos Crypto
question: Which change did the 2021 rulemaking make to the security research exemption, according to GitHub's summary?
options: It made circumvention tools legal to sell
It removed the condition that the research must not violate any other law
It ended the exemption
It extended the exemption to servers you do not own without permission
explain: GitHub explains that before 2021 a violation of another law such as the CFAA could also cost you the DMCA exemption. The Office recommended removing that condition, while noting researchers must still consider other laws themselves.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Professional ethics: ISC2, ACM, the Menlo Report and the UMN patches
question: Under the ISC2 complaint procedure, who may complain that a member breached Canon III (diligent and competent service to principals)?
options: Any member of the public
Only principals, meaning those with an employer or contractor relationship with the member
Only other certified professionals
Nobody: Canon III is advisory
explain: ISC2's procedure says anyone may complain about Canons I or II, only principals about Canon III, and only other professionals who subscribe to a code of ethics about Canon IV.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Why the pretraining mixture is a decision you cannot skip
question: Why is tuning the mixture directly on downstream benchmarks risky, beyond its cost?
options: Benchmarks are measured in accuracy, not loss
Downstream tuning always picks uniform weights
The mixture can overfit to the specific benchmarks used, which may not reflect the many tasks the model will face
explain: A pretrained model is used for many tasks nobody listed in advance. A mixture tuned to a handful of benchmarks can trade away performance elsewhere. DoReMi deliberately uses no downstream data.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Knobs, failure modes, and what came after DoReMi
question: You start DoReMi from uniform reference weights on a corpus where one domain is tiny. After one round, results are no better than baseline. What is the paper's recommended next move?
options: Run iterated DoReMi: train a new reference model on the round-1 weights and run again
Increase the proxy to 1B parameters
Set the smoothing c to 0 so weak domains disappear
Copy the published Pile weights
explain: On GLaM, round 1 from uniform weights was only comparable to the baseline, and round 2 matched downstream-tuned weights. A suboptimal reference gives a suboptimal excess loss; iterating fixes the reference. Bigger proxies did worse in the paper.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
question: Why do pipelines run heuristic rules before a perplexity filter or a model-based classifier?
options: Rules are more accurate than models
The order does not matter for cost
Rules only count words and symbols, so they cheaply remove obvious junk before the expensive model-based steps run
Perplexity filters only work on text that has been deduplicated
explain: A rule is a few counts per page; a language model or classifier must process every token. Removing describable junk first shrinks what the costly steps must score. Orders still vary between pipelines.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
question: In `soa<8> Point pts[...]` (float x, y, z), what is the byte offset of `pts[17].z` from the start of the array?
explain: Block 2 (17 divided by 8 is 2, rounded down), lane 1 (the remainder). Each block is 96 bytes and z is the third 32-byte run. Offset = 2 x 96 + 2 x 32 + 1 x 4 = 260. 212 is the AoS answer (17 x 12 + 8), 204 is where record 17 starts in AoS, and 68 is plain SoA (17 x 4).

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Finding sensitive data: inventories, patterns, checksums and context
question: A Purview-style rule finds a Luhn-valid 16-digit number with no keywords or dates within 300 characters. What should the confidence be?
options: Low: pattern and checksum without supporting context
High: the checksum proves it is a card
None: without a keyword it is discarded
High, because test numbers are excluded
explain: In Microsoft's documented definition, pattern plus checksum alone is the low-confidence pattern (65). High confidence (85) needs one of the context conditions. About 1 in 10 random numbers pass Luhn, so the checksum alone proves little.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Searching encrypted data: deterministic encryption and enclaves
question: A team wants to encrypt an `is_vip` boolean column but still filter on it. Why is deterministic encryption a poor choice?
options: Deterministic encryption cannot encrypt booleans
It is slower than randomized encryption
It requires a secure enclave
With only two values, each ciphertext appears in many rows, and counting them (plus any known fact about one row) reveals every row's value
explain: Deterministic encryption maps each plaintext to one ciphertext. With two possible values, there are two ciphertexts; knowing the VIP rate or one VIP customer decodes all rows. Microsoft's documentation warns about exactly this for True/False columns.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: How DLP recognises sensitive content
question: A DLP rule has 95% recall and a 1% false positive rate. Real leaks are 1 in 1,000 messages. Roughly what share of its alerts are real?
options: About 9%
About 95%
About 50%
About 1%
explain: Per 200,000 messages: 190 true alerts and about 1,998 false ones, so 190 / 2,188 is about 8.7%. Recall is 95%, but precision is low because clean messages vastly outnumber leaks.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Disposal as a process: Morgan Stanley's drives and the certificate
question: Branch servers had disk encryption switched on years after deployment, and the product encrypted only newly written data. Why does a later cryptographic erase not sanitise them?
options: The data written before encryption was enabled is still plaintext on the disks, and destroying the key does nothing to it
Crypto erase never works on servers
The keys were too short
Crypto erase needs internet access
explain: Cryptographic erase only removes access to what was encrypted. SP 800-88 Rev. 2 makes 'no sensitive data previously stored in plaintext' a precondition, and the SEC order describes exactly this flaw.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: What Internet honeypots see: noise, bots and reused passwords
question: Your new Internet-facing SSH honeypot logged 20,000 login attempts overnight. What is the right conclusion?
options: You are being targeted by a skilled group and should start incident response
Bots only try SSH, so other services are safe
The honeypot is misconfigured, since nobody knows its address
This is normal background noise; analyse it for trends rather than treating it as an incident
explain: Any public address is scanned constantly by automated tools. Volume alone says nothing about targeting; patterns, new exploits and overlap with your own logs do.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honey records and honeywords: decoys inside your data
question: You put a different honey record in each of four copies of a customer table. A trap address from the analytics copy starts receiving spam. What do you learn?
options: Nothing, honey records only show that some breach happened
That the analytics copy (or something it was exported to) leaked
That the production database is compromised
That the spam filter has failed
explain: Unique records per copy turn a late alert into a scoping clue: the leak path runs through the copy that held that record.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Measuring value: the Tularosa study, metrics and practice
question: In the Tularosa Study, what does "every participant in a Present condition triggered a decoy alert before reporting a successful exploit of a real machine" imply for defenders?
options: Decoy alerts gave warning before the real damage, which is the time a response team needs
Decoys prevented all exploitation
Participants recognised every decoy
Telling attackers about deception makes decoys useless
explain: The decoys did not stop every attack (exploit successes fell but were not zero); they consistently fired first, which is the early warning deception promises.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Seeds and RNG state: a different problem from kernels
question: Why does a counter-based hash of (seed, position, token id) beat a per-request stateful generator for reproducible sampling in a batched engine?
options: A hash produces higher-quality random numbers than a generator.
A hash makes the sampled token batch-invariant even when the kernels are not.
Each draw's noise is a pure function of the request's seed and the token's position, so it cannot depend on draw order, batch layout or how many draws came before.
A hash lets temperature 0 sample randomly.
explain: A generator, even a per-request one, hands out numbers in sequence, so the value used at a position depends on everything drawn earlier. A hash has no sequence. It does nothing for the logits: if the kernels move the logits, the argmax of logits plus noise can move too, so batch-invariant kernels are still needed. Quality and temperature 0 are not the point.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Why it matters: true on-policy RL and reproducible evaluation
question: Two teams report AIME'24 accuracy for the same BF16 checkpoint, each from one greedy run, 4 points apart. What should you ask before believing either number?
options: Which tokenizer version each team used, since greedy decoding is otherwise exact.
Their GPU type and count, TP size, batch size, dtype and engine settings, plus the spread across several runs: BF16 greedy accuracy alone can vary by several points across setups.
Whether either team set a random seed, since seeds control greedy outputs.
Nothing: a 4-point gap is far outside measurement noise.
explain: Greedy decoding uses no random numbers, so a seed does not help, and BF16 greedy results move with GPU count, type and batch size (a 9.15-point standard deviation on AIME'24 in the study). Report the setup and a spread over runs, or use FP32 for a single greedy run.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Knowing a run went wrong: invariants, oracles and liveness
question: Why is the cycle test's check (walk from key 0, expect N distinct keys) a stronger oracle than checking that each transaction returned success?
options: It runs faster than checking return codes
It never needs to read the database
It catches lost or interleaved writes even when every transaction reported success
It tests liveness instead of safety
explain: Isolation bugs typically return success while corrupting data. The ring property can only survive if every committed transaction behaved as if it ran alone, so it detects silent corruption that per-call results cannot. It is still a safety check.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Runners: where pipeline code runs, and how to isolate it
question: Which controls would have stopped the tj-actions payload from reading secrets on a GitHub-hosted runner, according to how it worked?
options: Masking secrets in the log
Running the job on a larger runner
Blocking egress and sudo, since the payload had to download its memory-dump script and run it as root
Pinning actions/checkout to a SHA
explain: Masking did not help because the payload base64-encoded the values twice. The payload needed network access to fetch memdump.py and root to read another process's memory. Pinning the compromised action itself would also have helped; pinning checkout does nothing.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Caches and artifacts: how Ultralytics was poisoned
question: Why could investigators tell that Ultralytics 8.3.45 was not built by the project's workflow?
options: Its version number was out of sequence
PyPI scans every upload for miners
It was larger than previous versions
It had no provenance attestation and no matching repository activity, unlike the releases from trusted publishing
explain: PyPI's write-up: the second round came from an unrevoked API token, which was detectable because there were no corresponding source repository activity or publish attestations.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Policy as code with OPA and Rego
question: Why pass the plan JSON to OPA rather than the raw HCL files?
options: OPA cannot read text files
The plan JSON contains resolved values and each resource's planned actions, so policy judges what will actually happen
HCL is not allowed in CI
The plan JSON is smaller
explain: OPA's Terraform guide works on the plan JSON because it shows resource_changes with resolved attributes and actions such as create or delete.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?
question: Why is autoregressive decoding slow on a GPU even though the GPU can do far more arithmetic per second than one token needs?
options: Each step must wait for the previous token, and each step does little compute per byte of weights read, so the GPU idles on memory traffic
Softmax over the vocabulary is the dominant cost and cannot be parallelized
The KV cache makes every step recompute attention over all earlier tokens from scratch
Causal attention needs more FLOPs than bidirectional attention
explain: Decode is sequential (token t+1 needs token t) and memory-bound: each pass streams all weights to process one token per sequence. A KV cache avoids recomputation; it does not create it. Causal attention actually computes fewer scores than bidirectional attention.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Build it: turn your GPT into a masked diffusion LM
question: In the run, low-confidence remasking at 128 steps reached a judge NLL of 1.447, close to real text's 1.413. What is the best reading?
options: The diffusion samples are now as good as real Shakespeare
Random remasking must have a bug, since it scored worse
The sampler commits the most predictable characters first and falls into repetition (diversity 0.111 against 0.516), which a judge model rewards, so the score overstates quality
More steps make diffusion samples worse
explain: A likelihood judge prefers predictable text, and repetition is predictable. The low diversity shows the samples are not like real text even though the judge scores them well. Random remasking is the exact reverse process; it is worse here because this small model's per-position marginals are poor, not because of a bug.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
question: System A serves 9 req/s on 3 GPUs at 92% attainment. System B serves 4 req/s on 1 GPU at 91% attainment, and 4.5 req/s at 85%. Assuming these are the largest rates meeting 90%, which has higher per-GPU goodput?
options: They tie, since both exceed 90%
A, because 9 req/s is more than 4 req/s
B, with 4 req/s per GPU against A's 3
B, with 4.5 req/s per GPU
explain: Per-GPU goodput divides the highest rate meeting the attainment goal by the GPU count: A gives 9/3 = 3 req/s per GPU and B gives 4/1 = 4. B's 4.5 req/s point misses the 90% goal, so it does not count.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
question: An offline batch job summarizes millions of documents overnight. There is no latency SLO; the goal is tokens per dollar. Which design do the sources point toward?
options: Separate prefill and decode clusters on different GPU generations, mandatory for throughput
Colocated serving with chunked prefill to keep every iteration near the compute-bound point
Disaggregation over 25 Gb/s Ethernet to save NVLink
Disaggregation, because it always raises goodput
explain: Goodput only matters when there are SLOs. DistServe's discussion says that in throughput-oriented offline settings, chunked prefill with piggybacking (decode tokens riding along in the batch of each prefill chunk) may be preferred because it fills each batch to the compute-bound threshold. vLLM's docs also note disaggregated prefill does not improve throughput.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: What deleting a file really does: a FAT walk-through
question: A deleted FAT file's entry says first cluster 3, size 5,000 bytes, 1,024-byte clusters. Unknown to you, the file was stored in clusters 3, 4, 9, 10 and 11. You recover 5,000 bytes from cluster 3 onward. What do you get?
options: The exact file, because FAT keeps a backup chain
The first 2,048 bytes correct, then whatever sits in clusters 5 to 7
Nothing, because a deleted entry has no first cluster
The exact file, because FAT never fragments files
explain: Clusters 3 and 4 are right (2,048 bytes). Deletion zeroed the chain, so the jump to 9 is lost and you read clusters 5, 6, 7 instead. The entry keeps the first cluster; there is no backup chain; and FAT files can fragment.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Linux ext4: superblock, inodes, extents and the journal
question: An ext4 image has 128-byte inodes. A colleague asks for each file's creation time. What do you answer?
options: 128-byte inodes have no creation time field; use other sources (journal, logs, application data) for when files appeared
Read crtime at offset 0x90
Use ctime, which is the creation time
Use dtime, which records the first write
explain: crtime exists only in the larger inode format. ctime is the inode change time, not creation (the prereq's backdating trick relies on that difference), and dtime is deletion time.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Shortcuts, Jump Lists, ShellBags and the Recycle Bin
question: An LNK file in Recent says its target was written 2026-03-02 14:01:07. The LNK file itself was created 2026-03-04 09:12. What can you say?
options: The target was modified on 4 March
The LNK file is forged because its dates disagree
The target was deleted on 4 March
When the shortcut was last updated, the target's write time was 2 March 14:01:07; the user most likely first opened it through this account on 4 March
explain: Header times describe the target as it was when the link was last updated; the LNK's own creation time reflects when the shortcut was made. Different dates are normal, not a sign of forgery.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics from the defender's side: what each trick leaves
question: Which observation is the strongest sign of deliberate anti-forensics rather than normal use?
options: Files in the Recycle Bin
Last-access times that are hours old
A Security log containing event 1102 shortly after an unusual administrator logon
Large free space on the disk
explain: Event 1102 records that the audit log was cleared, which ordinary users do not do, and timing next to an unusual admin logon raises it further. Recycle Bin items, lazy access times and free space are normal.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Vamana: RobustPrune and the alpha knob
question: In the toy example, alpha = 1.2 kept the edge p to E even though B is closer to E than p is. Which statement explains why that edge is useful?
options: E is p's nearest neighbor
Going through B would bring a search only slightly closer to E (5.00 vs 5.39), so a direct edge gives much faster progress toward points near E
Vamana keeps every edge longer than 5
alpha only affects the build pass, not which edges exist
explain: Under alpha = 1.2 an edge is dropped only if the detour node is closer to the target by a factor of 1.2 (for E: within 5.39 / 1.2 = 4.49). B is at 5.00, only about 7 percent closer, so the hop through B makes little progress. Keeping long edges where detours are weak is what shrinks the number of hops.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA: a fixed-degree graph built for GPUs
question: Why does CAGRA use rank-based reordering instead of computing distances between neighbors?
options: Ranks give strictly better graphs
Distance-based reordering needs about N x d_init x (d_init - 1) distance computations or an N x d_init distance table, which is slow or runs out of memory at scale
GPUs cannot compute distances
NN-descent does not produce sorted lists
explain: The paper reports that distance-based reordering was slower and hit out-of-memory on DEEP-100M, while rank-based reordering gave almost the same recall-throughput curve. The rank is a free proxy because NN-descent already sorted each list by distance.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: The DPO loss on one preference pair, with real numbers
question: A pair has policy log-probs chosen -30, rejected -20 and reference log-probs chosen -32, rejected -18, with $\beta = 0.1$. What is the DPO margin, and does the implicit reward rank the pair correctly?
options: -1.0, ranked wrong, because the policy gives the chosen answer lower probability
+0.4, ranked correctly, even though the policy still gives the chosen answer lower probability
+1.0, ranked correctly
0, because the reference and policy disagree
explain: Chosen log-ratio: -30 - (-32) = +2. Rejected: -20 - (-18) = -2. Margin 0.1 x (2 - (-2)) = +0.4, so the implicit reward ranks it correctly. Yet the policy itself still prefers the rejected text (-20 beats -30). DPO scores improvement relative to the reference, not raw likelihood; lesson 7 shows why this matters.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: ORPO and SimPO: dropping the reference model
question: A team must align a 7B base model on one GPU with tight memory and has paired preference data but no SFT checkpoint yet. Which method fits best?
options: DPO, because it is the most widely used
KTO, because it needs no pairs
ORPO, because it trains from the base model in one stage with no reference model
IPO, because it regularizes better
explain: ORPO combines the SFT loss with the odds-ratio penalty, so it needs neither a prior SFT stage nor a reference copy of the model. DPO, IPO and KTO all assume a reference (normally an SFT model) is available.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: How dual writes silently diverge, and how to contain it
question: A dual write does `old.increment(counter, 1)` then `new.increment(counter, 1)`, retrying the second call on timeout. After a week the new counters are slightly *higher* than the old ones. What is the most likely cause?
options: Clock skew between the two stores
A timed-out increment had actually been applied, so the retry applied it twice
The backfill copied counters that were already migrated
Last-writer-wins dropped some increments in the old store
explain: A timeout does not mean the write failed. Retrying a non-idempotent delta (add 1) after an ambiguous failure double-applies it. Writing the full current value read from the source of truth, or making the operation idempotent with a request ID, removes the problem.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: What end-to-end encryption promises, and against whom
question: A provider says its messages are "encrypted in transit and at rest". Which attacker can this design still let read messages?
options: Someone sniffing the café Wi-Fi
Nobody, since both transit and storage are encrypted
Only someone with the user's unlocked phone
The provider, or anyone who compromises or compels its servers
explain: In transit and at rest means the provider decrypts at its servers and holds the storage keys. Only end-to-end encryption keeps the keys off the server. The Wi-Fi sniffer is stopped by TLS; the unlocked phone is a device attacker that defeats any design.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: PQXDH: a post-quantum first message, and what formal analysis found
question: What did the PQXDH formal analysis show about adding a secure KEM to a secure protocol?
options: An encoding ambiguity between curve and KEM keys could weaken even the classical part, so formats must be disjoint
It can never make things worse
It made the protocol non-deniable
It removed the need for prekey signatures
explain: With ambiguous encodings the attacker can use one primitive against the other. The authors call it a cautionary tale for hybrids; Signal's spec now requires pairwise disjoint encodings.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Safety numbers: checking that the server gave you the right key
question: Why does Signal sort the two 30-digit halves before joining them?
options: To make the number shorter
To hide which key is newer
Sorting is needed for SHA-512
So both participants see the identical 60 digits, regardless of who is local and who is remote
explain: Each app computes its own half and the other person's half. Sorting gives one canonical order, so the two screens show the same number and a single comparison suffices.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: MLS ratchet trees: updating a big group in log n steps
question: In an 8-member MLS tree, member A commits an update. To which node does A encrypt the new root's path secret?
options: To every leaf E, F, G and H separately
To node EFGH, whose private key exactly E, F, G and H hold
To the server
To node ABCD
explain: The root's secret goes to the copath node on that level, EFGH. One ciphertext covers four members because they all know EFGH's private key by the tree invariant.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: When protocols broke: Matrix (2022) and Threema (2023)
question: Why did Element showing "Mallory joined the room" not count as a fix for the membership attack?
options: The message was encrypted
Mallory could not read messages
Element hid the event
Membership was still unauthenticated server data; in big rooms a join event goes unnoticed while clients send keys to the new member
explain: Detection by humans reading timelines does not scale. The keys flowed as soon as the server said Mallory was a member; the fix must stop that cryptographically.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Reviewing a secure messenger, and where to practise
question: A messenger uses the Signal protocol for content but lets its server add devices to accounts silently. Which review question exposes the risk?
options: 2, first key
6, metadata
8, assurance
5, who is in (device and group membership)
explain: Server-controlled device lists let the server enrol a reader, as in the Matrix device attack and linked-device phishing. The handshake and ratchet are fine; membership is not authenticated.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Maps: counting, histograms and timing in the kernel
question: A read takes exactly 1,024 ns. In which hist() bucket does it appear?
explain: 1024 = 2^10, so b = 10 and the bucket is [2^10, 2^11) = [1K, 2K). Bucket intervals include their lower bound and exclude their upper bound; only 0 and 1 get single-value buckets.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale
question: An activation tensor after ReLU has range [0, 6]. Using asymmetric int8 with q_min = -128, what are S and Z?
explain: S = (6 - 0) / (127 - (-128)) = 6/255 = 0.0235, and Z = round(-128 - 0/S) = -128. Real 0 maps to the lowest code, so all 256 levels cover [0, 6]. The symmetric choice (S = 6/127, Z = 0) would waste the 128 negative codes on values ReLU never produces.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
question: A wake-word model meets its accuracy target in float but loses 6 points after full-integer PTQ with per-channel weights. Calibration data is representative. What should you try next?
options: Quantization-aware training, or 16-bit activations if the runtime supports them
Per-tensor weights instead of per-channel
Remove calibration and use dynamic range quantization on a microcontroller with no float unit
Prune the model to 90% sparsity
explain: Per-channel weights and good calibration are already in place, so the remaining error likely comes from activations or from a small model's sensitivity. QAT lets the model adapt to rounding, and 16x8 mode reduces activation error. Per-tensor would be worse, and dynamic range keeps float outputs that an integer-only MCU cannot run.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Citrix Bleed, 2023: a length bug that leaked logged-in sessions
question: You installed the NetScaler fix on 11 October 2023, the day after it shipped. Why could an attacker still be using your gateway on 20 October?
options: The fix did not install
A session cookie stolen before the fix stayed valid until sessions were killed
The fix turned off MFA
NetScaler cannot be patched
explain: Exploitation began in late August. The fix stops new leaks but does not invalidate tokens already taken; NetScaler's guidance was to kill all active and persistent sessions after updating.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: The patch race: KEV-driven deadlines for edge devices
question: M-Trends 2026 estimates a mean time to exploit of -7 days. What does the negative sign mean for an edge patch process?
options: Patches arrive a week before bugs are found
On average, exploitation begins before a fix exists, so fast patching must be paired with checking for compromise that happened earlier
Attackers stopped using n-days
Vendors publish advisories a week late on purpose
explain: Negative TTE means exploitation precedes the patch. Speed still matters (it stops mass exploitation after disclosure), but forensic triage is what deals with the earlier window.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: End of support, hardening and the replace decision
question: Barracuda asked customers to replace ESG appliances 'regardless of patch version level'. What does that tell a defender about patching?
options: Patches from Barracuda were never released
Once an appliance may hold persistence the vendor cannot reliably remove, patching cannot restore trust; only new hardware can
Email gateways cannot be patched
Replacement is always cheaper than patching
explain: The patch fixed the bug, but the vendor could not be confident that software updates removed the intruder from compromised devices. The same logic drives rebuilds for Ivanti and hard resets for Cisco.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
question: A team trains with a hard rule 'reward = -1 if truncated at 8K tokens' and sees training become unstable as responses approach 8K. Which change follows the DAPO findings?
options: Raise the penalty to -10 so the model learns faster
Remove the correctness reward for long responses
Mask truncated samples from the loss, or ramp the penalty linearly over a soft zone before the limit
Lower the learning rate only for long responses
explain: Overlong filtering (masking) and soft overlong punishment both reduce reward noise from punishing reasoning that was merely cut off. A bigger cliff adds more noise, not less.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: One input, many readers: where encoding bugs come from
question: A gateway blocks paths containing `..`; the app behind it percent-decodes the path and opens the file. Which change actually closes the hole?
options: Make the gateway also block the string `%2e%2e`
Lower-case the path in the gateway before checking
In the app, decode, resolve the full path and check it is inside the base folder before opening
Return a generic error page so attackers learn less
explain: Blocking one encoded spelling leaves the others (`%2E%2e`, double encoding, and more). Resolving and checking the final path in the component that opens the file covers every spelling, because the decision is made on what the path finally means.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Unicode normalisation: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD
question: Which pair is canonically equivalent (so equal after NFC), not just compatibility equivalent?
options: `ﬁ` (U+FB01) and `fi`
`／` (U+FF0F) and `/`
Ω OHM SIGN (U+2126) and Ω GREEK CAPITAL LETTER OMEGA (U+03A9)
explain: UAX #15 lists the ohm sign as a canonical singleton: it never survives normalisation, even NFC. The ligature, fullwidth solidus and superscript five are compatibility equivalents and change only under NFKC or NFKD.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Confusables and homoglyphs: UTS #39 skeletons
question: `ѕсоре` is written entirely in Cyrillic and `scope` entirely in Latin. Which check flags the pair?
options: A mixed-script check on each string
Comparing their NFKC forms
Comparing their UTS #39 skeletons
Comparing them after `casefold()`
explain: Each string is single-script, so a mixed-script rule passes both. NFKC and case folding leave Cyrillic letters Cyrillic. Only the skeleton, which maps Cyrillic ѕ, с, о, р, е to Latin prototypes, shows they look the same.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: JSON differentials: duplicate keys, numbers and CouchDB
question: Two services read the same JSON body. Service A keeps the first value of a duplicate key, service B the last. Which design removes the disagreement?
options: Reject documents with duplicate keys at the entry point, then forward the parsed object or a canonical re-serialisation
Tell clients not to send duplicates
Make both services keep the first value, by convention
Sort the keys alphabetically
explain: Asking clients to behave does nothing against an attacker. Aligning two parsers by convention breaks again when a library changes. Rejecting at the edge and forwarding only unambiguous data means there is nothing to disagree about.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Defender's checklist for encodings and parsers, and where to practise
question: You find that your login redirect check and the browser disagree on hosts for URLs containing backslashes. After fixing the code, what is the most important next step?
options: Search logs for past redirect parameters whose parsed hosts differed, and review the sessions involved
Close the ticket
Rotate the TLS certificate
Disable all redirects permanently
explain: A differential may have been used before you found it. Replaying stored raw inputs through both parsers tells you whether anyone was sent off-site, which decides the rest of the response.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Sysmon configuration: include, exclude and rule groups
question: A NetworkConnect filter is `onmatch="include"` with two rules: Image ends with `powershell.exe`, and DestinationPort is `443`. Which connection is logged?
options: Only connections made by powershell.exe to port 443
Any connection made by powershell.exe
Any connection to port 443
Every connection, because include with two rules logs all
explain: The two rules are on different fields (Image and DestinationPort), and Sysmon combines different fields with AND. Two rules on the same field would have been ORed.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control I: allowlisting and AppLocker
question: Your draft AppLocker policy has run in audit mode for two weeks. Which events tell you what the policy would have broken?
explain: 8003 (EXE or DLL) and 8006 (script or MSI) mean 'allowed, but would have been prevented if enforced', and appear only in audit mode. 8004 and 8007 are actual blocks in enforce mode; 8002 and 8005 are allows.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: What EDR can and cannot see
question: An attacker uses only built-in tools (net for accounts and shares, wmic, and ntdsutil, the Active Directory database tool) with valid admin credentials. Why is this hard for an EDR?
options: The telemetry is recorded, but each action resembles normal administration, so detection depends on context and baselines rather than a 'malware' verdict
EDR cannot record built-in tools
Built-in tools disable EDR automatically
Windows hides admin activity from all sensors
explain: The sensor still records the processes and command lines. The difficulty is deciding they are malicious: CISA's living-off-the-land guidance notes that many organisations lack the capabilities to tell such activity from normal administration, which is why baselines of admin behaviour matter.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
question: At minute 47 the meter reads 122 W. Which statement is correct using only that one reading?
options: It must be the fridge, because the fridge draws 120 W
It could be the fridge alone, or two 60 W lamps if the house had two, so one reading cannot decide
It must be the lamp plus 62 W of noise
It is the kettle in a low-power state
explain: A single reading only constrains the sum. With three known appliances, 120 W happens to match one combination, but adding a second 60 W lamp would create a second exact match. Context over time (what changed, and when) is what breaks such ties.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem
question: A model reaches F1 0.95 on houses it was trained on and 0.60 on a new house. What is the most useful next step suggested by this course's sources?
options: Report 0.95, since the training houses are representative
Shrink the window to one sample to avoid overfitting
Switch to CO, which needs no training data
Add synthetic aggregates built from activations of many houses and evaluate on a held-out house
explain: Kelly and Knottenbelt found that mixing synthetic aggregates with real data regularised the nets and helped on unseen houses, and both they and Zhang and colleagues test on a held-out house. A one-sample window throws away the context that makes neural NILM work, and CO still needs appliance models learned from sub-metered data.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
question: Why is a missing domain scored as weight 0 rather than with the disagree weight -2.74?
options: Missing data carries no evidence either way; scoring it as disagreement would push true duplicates like r1-r3 toward non-match
Because log2 of zero is undefined
Because Fellegi-Sunter only allows agreement levels
explain: A missing value is neither agreement nor disagreement. Treating it as disagreement subtracts 2.74 and would drop r1-r3 from 0.863 to about 0.49, punishing incomplete records rather than conflicting ones.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Evaluating entity resolution: labels, pairwise and cluster metrics
question: Why is labelling 1,000 uniformly random record pairs a poor way to evaluate a deduplication system?
options: Almost all random pairs are non-matches (about 1 in 1,000 match in FEBRL1), so you learn almost nothing about recall or about the uncertain pairs
Random pairs are too hard for people to label
Random sampling is biased toward large clusters
Labels must come from the same blocks as training
explain: Matches are a tiny fraction of all pairs, so a random sample is nearly all easy non-matches. Stratify candidate pairs by score band, or label whole clusters, to put the labelling effort where errors happen.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
question: A tenant has 3 Global Administrators, all eligible through PIM, but 14 users hold Application Administrator permanently, and one app they manage has the Graph permission RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory. What is the real number of paths to Global Administrator power?
options: 3: only the Global Administrators
0: PIM eligibility blocks all paths
14: but only if those users also hold Helpdesk Administrator
At least 17: any Application Administrator can add a credential to that app and use its permission to assign roles
explain: Microsoft's role reference warns that Application Administrators can add credentials to an app and act as it. An app with RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory can assign roles, so each of the 14 is a path, plus the 3 eligible admins.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
question: A thief steals a refresh token issued to a mail client that Ana consented to for Mail.Read and Files.Read. What can the thief obtain?
options: Only mail access tokens, because the token was issued for Exchange
Nothing without Ana's MFA
Only an ID token
Access tokens for any resource the client was granted for Ana, including files
explain: Microsoft documents refresh tokens as bound to user and client, not to a resource. The client can redeem it for access tokens to any resource where it holds permission, and the MFA claim from Ana's original sign-in carries over.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
question: A tenant's only Conditional Access policy requires MFA for 'All users' and excludes the group 'Service Accounts'. An attacker sprays passwords. Which account is the most valuable target?
options: A regular user, because MFA is optional for them
The emergency access account, because it has no MFA
A guest user
An account in 'Service Accounts': a correct password is enough, because no policy applies to it
explain: Excluded accounts are evaluated by no policy, so a sprayed password suffices. Emergency accounts should be protected by a phishing-resistant credential, not by Conditional Access; service accounts need managed identities or workload policies instead.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A hardening baseline, an incident runbook, and where to practise
question: During an incident you find a malicious multitenant app with Mail.Read (application) in your tenant. What is the right first action on the app?
options: Delete the app's service principal
Reset the passwords of all users
Ask the app's publisher to delete the application object
Disable the service principal so it cannot obtain tokens or be consented to again, then remove its grants and investigate what it read
explain: Microsoft's consent playbook says to disable rather than delete: a deleted service principal can return when someone consents again, while a disabled one cannot get tokens. Then remove its grants and scope its access in the logs.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
question: An ET server reads one 4096-byte chunk per event and then returns to epoll_wait. A client uploads 10,000 bytes in one burst and waits for a reply. What happens?
options: The server reads all 10,000 bytes over three wakeups
epoll_wait returns EAGAIN
The kernel splits the burst into three separate edge events
The server reads 4096 bytes and may never be woken for the remaining 5904, so the client hangs
explain: Once all the bytes are queued, nothing new arrives after the first 4096 are read, so there is no new edge, and epoll_wait can block forever with 5904 bytes in the buffer. This is exactly step 5 of the epoll(7) example. Fix: read until EAGAIN, or until a short read on a stream socket.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set
question: Your team trains a learned reranker on click logs from January to June and evaluates on 300 labeled queries sampled from the same months. Which leak is most likely to inflate the test score?
options: The test queries use graded rather than binary labels
Many test queries, or close paraphrases of them, also appear in the training clicks
The test set is too large for a bootstrap confidence interval
The reranker uses a cross-encoder instead of a bi-encoder
explain: Popular queries repeat. A reranker trained on clicks for a query has effectively seen its answer. Split by query cluster and preferably by time (train on earlier months, test on later), so test queries are genuinely new. A 300-query set is not too large to bootstrap (lesson 4), and the reranker's design (a cross-encoder reads query and document together, a bi-encoder embeds each separately) does not create a leak.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Stack canaries: a tripwire in front of the return address
question: Why does the compiler insert the canary check just before `ret` rather than right after `strcpy`?
options: Because strcpy itself checks the canary
Because the return address is only used at ret, so checking just before it guards that use whatever code wrote to the frame
Because the check is free at ret but costly elsewhere
Because the canary is only written at the end of the function
explain: The canary protects the return address, and the return address is only consumed by ret. Checking just before ret covers every write that happened anywhere in the function body, not just one call. The cost is the same anywhere; strcpy knows nothing about canaries.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: RELRO, the GOT and FORTIFY_SOURCE
question: A binary is built with partial RELRO only. An attacker has a bug that writes 8 chosen bytes to a chosen address. Which table is still a useful target, and which flag closes it?
options: The stack canary; -fstack-protector-all
The PLT stubs; -Wl,-z,noexecstack
.got.plt, left writable for lazy binding; -Wl,-z,now (full RELRO)
.text; -fPIE
explain: Partial RELRO leaves .got.plt writable so lazy binding can fill it in. Adding -z now makes the loader resolve everything at start-up so the whole GOT can be made read-only.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Kernel mitigations: SMEP, SMAP, KASLR, KPTI and EternalBlue
question: According to Microsoft's analysis, which change made EternalBlue as leaked fail on the newest 64-bit Windows 10 even before patching?
options: The HAL region it relied on was no longer executable and its address was randomized
SMBv1 was removed from Windows 10
Windows 10 used stack canaries in the kernel
The NSA patched the exploit
explain: The exploit placed its payload in the HAL region at a known, executable address, which held on Windows 7. Windows 10 made that memory non-executable and the latest 64-bit builds randomized it. The SMBv1 bug itself remained until MS17-010 was applied.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
question: Two threads write different fields of one struct that fits in a single cache line. A colleague says this cannot be slow because nothing is shared. What is the best reply?
options: Right, the compiler places each field on its own line automatically
Right, only atomic variables can cause cache contention
Wrong, but only because the struct needs a mutex
Wrong, the fields share one cache line, so each write forces the line to move between cores
explain: Compilers pack fields together to save space; they do not spread them across lines. Any write needs the whole line, so the two cores fight over it. No mutex is needed for correctness here, because the fields are distinct; the problem is purely performance.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: How big is a line, how to find false sharing, who pads
question: Why might a library avoid the C++17 constant `hardware_destructive_interference_size` in a public header?
options: Its value can change with compiler tuning flags, so separately built code may disagree on struct layout
It is not defined in C++17
It is always 64, which is too small
It only works with std::atomic members
explain: GCC sets it from -mtune, and its documentation warns that all translation units relying on it must use the same tuning. In a public header that is an ABI hazard, so libraries often use a fixed constant such as 128 instead.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Cheaper rounds and smarter servers: compression and FedOpt
question: On the skewed split with E = 5, a colleague replaces FedAvg with a well-tuned FedAdam and expects the toy to reach 2.3. Where does it converge, if it converges?
options: To 2.3, because adaptive steps correct client drift
To about 1.944, the same fixed point, because the averaged delta is zero there whatever the server does
To 1.667, the average of the local optima
It cannot converge, since Adam needs true gradients
explain: At 1.944 the clients' moves cancel in the weighted average, so the pseudo-gradient is zero and every server optimizer stops there. Server optimizers change speed and stability. To move the destination you must change what clients compute: less local work, a proximal term, or SCAFFOLD's control variates (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Threats: what updates leak and how clients poison the model
question: An auditor argues that FedAvg's 5 local epochs per round make client updates safe to share in the clear. Based on the Inverting Gradients experiments, what is the best reply?
options: Correct: after 5 epochs the update no longer depends on individual examples
Correct only for convolutional networks
Wrong: 5 local epochs were no harder to invert than 1; only more images per update made reconstruction harder, and not safe
Wrong, because local epochs make updates larger and therefore easier to invert
explain: Geiping et al. found single-image reconstructions unimpeded even after 100 local steps, and their 8-image experiments were no harder at 5 epochs than at 1. Averaging over more images lowered quality, but some images from a batch of 100 were still recognizable. Formal protection needs differential privacy.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-gamma: expand every neighbor list by gamma
question: Why does ACORN-gamma skip HNSW's RNG-based pruning when building neighbor lists?
options: It makes construction too slow
The pruned detour through a third node may fail the predicate, so the shortcut it relied on vanishes in the predicate subgraph
RNG pruning only works for cosine distance
HNSW never prunes at the bottom level
explain: HNSW drops edge v to b if some kept neighbor a is closer to b, trusting search to go v, a, b. For a predicate where v and b pass but a fails, that path does not exist. Without knowing predicates at build time you cannot prune safely, so ACORN keeps the near neighbors and uses a predicate-agnostic compression instead.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Fine-grained experts: split each expert into m slices
question: You split each of 16 experts into 4 (64 experts total) but forget to change top-2 routing. What happens?
options: Per-token expert compute drops to one quarter, because 2 small experts are only half of one original expert
Nothing changes; the layer has the same parameters and FLOPs
Per-token compute rises 4 times because there are 4 times as many experts
The router stops working because softmax needs exactly 16 outputs
explain: Segmentation keeps compute constant only if you also raise the number of active experts from K to mK, here from 2 to 8. With top-2 of 64 quarter-size experts, each token uses 2/4 = 0.5 of one original expert instead of 2, a quarter of the FLOPs. Total parameters are unchanged.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Aux-loss-free balancing: steer the router with a bias
question: Why does Algorithm 1 use sign(e) rather than e itself?
options: The paper tried b += u x e and found it slightly better balanced but no better in perplexity, so it kept the simpler sign rule
sign(e) is required for causality
Using e would make the bias receive gradients
sign(e) guarantees exact balance every step
explain: Table 3 of the paper compares variants: the proportional rule reached MaxVio 0.028 to 0.040 with perplexity 9.51 to 9.53, versus 0.044 and 9.50 for the sign rule with u = 0.001. Neither variant involves gradients or future tokens.
